question: Q01
answer: In the housing exercise (note-gradient-descent-from-scratch, sheet02) the learning rate eta = 0.1 blew up on the raw features: the loss exploded to inf within 12 steps (eta = 0.001 converged but needed ~40,000 iterations; eta = 0.01 was the best compromise on raw features). What fixed it (update 2026-05-19) was not a different learning rate but feature scaling: after standardizing every feature (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) eta = 0.1 converged in under 200 iterations. Your lesson: 'before blaming the learning rate, look at the feature scales.'

question: Q03
answer: Three notes together make the argument: note-gaussian-noise-least-squares (Gaussian noise on y makes maximum likelihood equal to minimizing the sum of squared residuals, with a 1/(2σ²) factor), note-map-estimation-priors (MAP = log-likelihood + log-prior; an isotropic Gaussian prior θ ~ N(0, τ²I) contributes −‖θ‖²/(2τ²), so with the Gaussian-noise linear model the objective is squared error plus a constant times ‖θ‖², the constant being σ²/τ²), and note-ridge-regression-penalty (ridge minimizes ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖², closed form (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy). Link: if you assume Gaussian noise with variance σ² and put a zero-mean Gaussian prior with variance τ² on the weights, then the MAP estimate minimizes (1/(2σ²))‖y − Xw‖² + (1/(2τ²))‖w‖²; multiplying by 2σ² gives exactly the ridge objective with λ = σ²/τ². So the L2 penalty is the negative log of a Gaussian prior: a narrow prior (small τ) means a large λ and strong shrinkage, a flat prior (τ → ∞) means λ → 0 and plain least squares/MLE. This also answers the open question in your ridge note ('Where does λ come from ... does it mean something?') — though none of your notes states that connection explicitly or links the ridge note to the MAP note; the MAP note's Laplace-prior remark gives the lasso analogue.

evidence.quote: L(w) = ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖²
Where does λ come from — is it just a knob you tune by cross-validation, or does it mean something?
the whole thing is squared error plus a constant times ‖θ‖², with the constant being σ²/τ² after rescaling.
argmax_w log L(w) = argmin_w Σ_i (y_i − wᵀx_i)²

question: Q04
answer: Current view (note-p-values-corrected, 2026-06-18, state evolving): a p-value is P(test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed | H0 true) — computed assuming H0, not P(H0 | data); a large p does not show H0 is true, p = 0.03 is not '3% chance the null is right', and tiny p with a huge sample can go with an irrelevant effect, so report effect size and a CI. Your working reading: 'if nothing were going on, data this extreme would show up about 3% of the time'. Yes, you believed something different before: note-p-values-first-take (2026-04-22, now state deprecated) said 'A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true. So p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance H0 is right' and 'Large p → H0 true'. The corrected note opens with 'I had this wrong in April' and cites the ASA 2016 statement.

evidence.quote: p = P(test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed | H0 is true)
A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
I had this wrong in April.
